analysis.one_liner: Requires groups spending on elections to name their big donors within 24 hours and closes foreign-money loopholes.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 46 Democratic and independent Senate cosponsors and no Republican support, the bill sits in the Senate Rules Committee without a scheduled vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The DISCLOSE Act would require corporations, unions, super PACs, and dark-money nonprofit groups that spend more than $10,000 influencing an election to report those expenditures to the Federal Election Commission within 24 hours and identify anyone who gave them $10,000 or more. Political ads would have to name the group's top five funders on screen, and the bill would extend the ban on foreign money in elections to digital ads, judicial-nomination campaigns, and state ballot measures. It would also make it a crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, to set up a company to hide foreign election money.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters. Today, groups that spend unlimited money on elections — super PACs and tax-exempt 'social welfare' nonprofits — can often do so without ever naming their donors. This bill would force that money into the open within a day, put the top five funders of an ad on the ad itself, and close pathways foreign money can use to reach U.S. campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting to know who funds ads

how_it_helps.text: Covered organizations that spend more than $10,000 on campaign activity in an election cycle must file a report with the FEC within 24 hours listing their beneficial owners and identifying every person who gave them $10,000 or more.

Political ads paid for with campaign-related money would have to display a 'stand by every ad' statement naming the top five funders of the group paying for it, with a shorter top-two list for audio ads.

The foreign-money ban would be extended to paid digital ads, internet activity, and communications about federal judicial nominations, and foreign government money would be barred from state and local ballot initiative and referendum campaigns.

Setting up or using a corporation or other entity with the intent to conceal a foreign national's election spending would become a crime carrying up to five years in prison, and the GAO would have to study and report on illicit foreign money in each four-year election cycle.

analysis.who_pays: Groups that currently spend on elections anonymously — super PACs, 501(c)(4) 'social welfare' organizations, trade associations, and corporations — would lose the ability to keep donors hidden, and would bear new reporting costs. Large online platforms would have to carry the expanded disclaimers on political ads.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dark-money groups, super PACs, and big platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill applies its disclosure regime to labor organizations as well as corporations, so unions would bear the same 24-hour reporting and donor-identification duties.

Donors could face exposure; the bill responds by creating an exemption for people who show specific evidence that disclosure would subject them to serious threats, harassment, or reprisals, and it lets donors forbid in writing that their money be used for campaign spending.

The bill leans on the FEC and the courts to make disclosure work — it orders the FEC to write regulations and routes all constitutional challenges to the D.C. federal courts — so its real-world effect depends on enforcement and on litigation over how far disclosure can go.
Compliance costs fall on a wide range of groups, including small nonprofits, and platforms over 50 million monthly U.S. users would bear new ad-disclaimer obligations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is transparency against the burden of reporting and the exposure of donors. The bill's own text acknowledges the exposure risk and builds in a harassment exemption and a written opt-out for donors who don't want their money spent on campaigns. The compliance burden is real but modest compared with the sums involved — the bill's findings cite an estimated $1.05 billion in dark-money spending in the 2020 cycle. The larger uncertainty is whether enforcement agencies and courts will make the rules stick.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 4, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, where it has sat without a markup or a vote; the Congress is still in session, so it is not yet dead.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill with 47 total cosponsors listed on the bill text — 44 Democrats and 2 independents among the 46 additional cosponsors — and no Republicans.
The Senate referred the bill to the Committee on Rules and Administration on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no further activity since then.

The bill's findings state that dark-money groups spent an estimated $1,050,000,000 in the 2020 election cycle and that one nonprofit alone spent nearly $40,000,000 on ads about Supreme Court nominees since 2016 without disclosure requirements.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the groups that spend election money anonymously — super PACs and donor-hidden nonprofits — are better off, because nothing has changed and no disclosure is coming from this bill.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DISCLOSE Act of 2026 in the Senate on March 4, 2026.

for.name: Senate Democratic and independent cosponsors (46)
for.role: Cosponsors including Sens. Schumer, Durbin, Klobuchar, Warren, Sanders and King
for.what_they_did: All 46 cosponsors signed on; they are Democrats and independents, including both independents who caucus with Democrats.

against.name: Sen. Deb Fischer
against.role: Chair, Senate Rules and Administration Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee she chairs received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it; no markup or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Sen. John Thune
against.what_they_did: Controls the Senate floor calendar; the bill has not been brought up for consideration, and no Republican has cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 46 cosponsors is a Democrat or an independent who cautions with Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and with Republicans holding the Senate majority the bill faces a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: Dark-money nonprofits (501(c)(4) 'social welfare' groups and 501(c)(6) business leagues)
industries.note: These groups can currently spend heavily on elections and judicial-nomination fights without naming donors; the bill would require them to identify their large donors within 24 hours, ending the anonymity that is their main advantage. Their interest in staying hidden runs directly against voters' interest in knowing who is paying for the ads they see.

industries.industry: Super PACs and other political spending committees
industries.note: Super PACs can accept unlimited contributions from any non-foreign source; the bill would force 24-hour expenditure reports and put their top five funders on the screen of every ad they run. Their stake is in keeping funders concealed, which conflicts with the public's interest in attribution.

industries.industry: Corporations and trade associations spending on elections
industries.note: The bill would require corporations to disclose beneficial owners and large funders when they finance campaign communications, and it would extend the foreign-money ban to entities used to conceal foreign money. Companies that currently influence elections invisibly would operate in public view.

Unions are covered organizations under the bill, so they would bear the same 24-hour reporting and donor-identification duties as corporations. Unlike corporate dark money, union money generally comes from identifiable dues, so the practical loss is compliance burden more than secrecy.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (50M+ U.S. monthly users)
industries.note: The bill defines covered online platforms and requires their political ads to carry expanded disclaimers naming top funders, with adapted-disclaimer options for short or digital formats. This is a compliance obligation on ad operations rather than a ban, and platforms have generally resisted friction on political advertising.

industries.industry: Foreign nationals seeking to influence U.S. elections
industries.note: The bill extends the foreign-money ban to paid digital communications, internet activity, judicial-nomination ads, and ballot-measure campaigns by covered foreign nationals, and criminalizes using a company to hide foreign money. Their gain from access runs against the integrity of U.S. elections.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the Senate majority, a Republican chairing the Rules Committee, and zero Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or a floor vote in this Congress — the same pattern that has repeatedly buried past versions of the DISCLOSE Act in committee. Its main near-term value to supporters is as a statement of position heading into the 2026 midterms.
